output.catalog_implications: Evidence: classify bench press and standard push-up as related horizontal-pressing patterns with shoulder horizontal flexion/adduction and elbow extension demands, while retaining open-chain versus closed-chain and external-load-versus-body-load fields. Inference: a planning model may allow provisional substitution when the catalog records load method, hand width, depth/ROM, tempo, and stability constraints; it should not assume equal repetitions, fatigue cost, or skill transfer. Evidence: record narrow, shoulder-width, and wide push-up hand placements as meaningful variants because EMG changes with hand base, but do not label any placement as muscle-isolating. Inference: use hand width and shoulder-abduction angle as technique/load modifiers and attach a shoulder-demand flag rather than an automatic injury-risk label. Evidence: shortened bench-press ROM raises apparent strength and changes the sticking-region/load-velocity profile. Inference: store ROM explicitly and prohibit direct comparison of 1RM, velocity, or progression targets across full-, partial-, and board/limited-ROM variants without recalibration. Evidence: higher EMG or modeled joint load does not by itself prove greater hypertrophy, performance transfer, or injury incidence; no cited source supports a sport-skill-production claim. Limits: most studies used young, trained, predominantly male samples, acute or cross-sectional designs, small samples, and controlled techniques; push-up results may not generalize to incline, decline, unstable, plyometric, deficit, or fatigue-to-failure variants, and the 2024 shoulder model used light loads and modeled rather than directly measured internal forces.
output.direct_findings: [S1] In experienced resistance-trained men, push-ups and bench presses performed across comparable loading conditions showed no significant differences in measured kinematics or activation of the examined upper-body muscles; weight-vest push-ups can therefore reproduce several bench-press loading conditions, but the study used matched depth/hand width and does not establish universal equivalence. [S2] At a load matched to the push-up body-mass resistance, participants completed substantially more push-up than bench-press repetitions to failure; the authors attribute practical differences to task constraints including closed- versus open-chain mechanics, trunk stabilization, barbell control, and excursion. [S2] The study observed phase- and muscle-specific EMG differences, including lower triceps activity in the push-up concentric phase and lower anterior-deltoid activity in the bench-press eccentric phase; EMG is not a direct measure of hypertrophy or joint force. [S3] Narrow-base push-ups elicited greater pectoralis-major and triceps-brachii EMG than wide-base push-ups in the tested sample, supporting a catalog distinction for hand-width variants rather than a claim that they isolate one muscle. [S4] Across 14 bench-press EMG studies, pectoralis major and triceps activity was generally greater than anterior-deltoid activity, while activation changed with intensity, movement velocity, fatigue, movement phase, mental focus, and stability. [S4] The review identifies substantial methodological limits in surface EMG normalization, electrode/measurement practice, and muscle-model interpretation. [S5] Reducing bench-press ROM increased 1RM and altered velocity profiles and the propulsive/braking contribution; the sticking-region pattern was clearest in full ROM, so ROM-specific strength and velocity data should not be treated as interchangeable. [S6] In ten experienced lifters using a light 16-kg bar, grip width, shoulder-abduction angle, scapular pose, and mediolateral bar forces changed modeled shoulder reaction loads; narrower grips and scapular retraction reduced selected AC compression, posterior GH shear, and modeled rotator-cuff activity. The authors report potential injury-risk implications, not prospective injury reduction.

results.input: Vertical pressing and shoulder isolation variations

output.catalog_implications: Evidence-supported fields: classify vertical presses as multi-joint shoulder-elevation exercises with scapular upward rotation, humeral abduction/flexion components, elbow extension, and meaningful deltoid/triceps/trapezius involvement; classify lateral raises as primarily shoulder-abduction isolations and frontal raises as shoulder-flexion isolations with different deltoid-head emphases. Evidence supports separate tags for front versus back bar path, free-weight versus machine stabilization demand, grip/humeral-rotation orientation, elbow-flexed versus extended lever, and concentric versus eccentric phase. Evidence supports recording ROM and whether the exercise reaches high elevation, but it does not establish one universally optimal or universally safe ROM for every shoulder. Planning-model inference: use presses earlier when heavier loading and system-wide strength are priorities, then use raises for lower-load, head-specific volume; treat machine presses as potentially less stabilization-demanding rather than automatically inferior. Treat EMG as an acute activation proxy, not proof of superior long-term hypertrophy, strength transfer, or sport-skill production. Limits: the key EMG studies used very small samples of healthy, experienced male bodybuilders or resistance-trained men, often one set and controlled loads; findings may not generalize to novices, women, injured shoulders, or ordinary programming. Back-press safety claims should not be generalized beyond participants with adequate shoulder ROM and trunk control, and no cited source supports a sport-skill claim.
output.direct_findings: [S1] Overhead pressing combines scapular upward rotation, humeral abduction and elbow extension, engaging deltoids, upper trapezius, pectoralis major and triceps. In eight competitive bodybuilders, back-barbell pressing produced greater medial/posterior-deltoid EMG than front-barbell pressing, while front-barbell pressing produced greater pectoralis-major EMG; barbell variants generally required more stabilizing-muscle excitation than machine variants. [S2] In ten competitive bodybuilders, neutral-grip lateral raises produced greater medial-deltoid EMG than externally rotated, frontal-raise and flexed-elbow variants; internally rotated lateral raises increased posterior-deltoid, upper-trapezius and triceps EMG, while frontal raises emphasized anterior deltoid and pectoralis major. [S3] In thirteen resistance-trained men at 60% 1RM for 12 repetitions, shoulder press showed the greatest anterior-deltoid activation among tested exercises, and shoulder press and lateral raise showed higher medial-deltoid activation than bench press and dumbbell fly; lateral raise showed the highest posterior-deltoid activation. [S4] Deltoid contribution to maximal shoulder flexion/abduction strength increased with elevation angle, reported as approximately 24% at 0 degrees and 75% at 120 degrees in the tested conditions. [S5] Across resistance-training studies, full ROM generally favored strength outcomes over partial ROM, but hypertrophy conclusions were more heterogeneous and depend on the muscle length and ROM region trained. [S6] The ACSM position stand supports both single- and multiple-joint exercises, recommends sequencing multi-joint exercises before single-joint work when preserving intensity is important, and recommends loading, volume and rest periods according to training status and goal.
output.exercise_family: Vertical pressing and shoulder isolation variations

results.input: Rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, and upper-back pulling

output.catalog_implications: Evidence-backed catalog fields should distinguish movement pattern (horizontal pull/row versus vertical pull/pulldown or pull-up), implement (free weight, cable, machine, bodyweight), grip orientation (pronated, supinated, neutral), grip width, support/stability, unilateral versus bilateral execution, torso position, and whether the exercise is externally loadable or limited by body mass and grip strength. The mechanics model should tag the primary joint actions as shoulder adduction/extension with scapular retraction/depression contributions and elbow flexion, while treating muscle emphasis as task- and technique-dependent rather than exclusive. Fenwick et al. support a high-confidence practical tradeoff field: supported/inverted rows can provide substantial upper-back and lat stimulus with less lumbar loading, bent-over rows impose more isometric trunk and lumbar demand, and one-arm cable rows add anti-rotation demand; these are evidence-based inferences from one small male sample, not universal rankings. Full-ROM execution should be the default planning label when pain-free and technically controlled, with partial ROM represented as a purposeful modification for load, tolerance, or fatigue management; the ROM meta-analysis is mostly lower-body and should not be overgeneralized to pulldowns or rows. Pull-ups should be tagged as closed-chain, relative-load movements with higher whole-body and often grip/arm-demand constraints than cable pulldowns; pulldowns permit finer load scaling and are therefore more practical for novice, high-volume, or fatigue-managed programming. EMG findings can calibrate likely acute recruitment and technique differences, but they should not be converted into claims of greater hypertrophy, strength, injury prevention, rehabilitation superiority, or sport-skill transfer without longitudinal or task-specific evidence. Limits include small samples, predominantly healthy men, acute surface EMG rather than long-term outcomes, exercise-specific technique, and incomplete evidence on fatigue across sets; avoid implying that any grip or exercise is universally safest or best.
output.direct_findings: [Fenwick et al. 2009] In seven healthy men, the inverted row produced the highest latissimus dorsi, upper-back, and hip-extensor activation among the inverted row, standing bent-over row, and standing one-arm cable row, with lower lumbar-erector activation and lower measured spinal load; the bent-over row produced the largest lumbar spine load and stiffness, while the one-arm cable row challenged trunk torsional capacity. [Doma et al. 2013] Chin-ups and lat pulldowns both emphasized latissimus dorsi and biceps brachii, but chin-ups showed greater concentric biceps/erector-spinae EMG and greater shoulder/C7 kinematic values than pulldowns; the study did not establish superior long-term adaptation or sport transfer. [Lusk et al. 2010] At 70% 1RM with controlled 2-second concentric and eccentric phases, a pronated anterior lat pulldown elicited greater latissimus dorsi EMG than a supinated grip, while grip width did not significantly alter latissimus, middle-trapezius, or biceps EMG in the tested wide-versus-bi-acromial conditions. [Andersen et al. 2014] In 15 men performing 6RM lat pulldowns with narrow, medium, and wide grips, grip width was directly tested as a strength and activation variable; this supports cataloging grip width as a manipulable loading/comfort field rather than assuming that wider automatically means more lat stimulus. [Pérez-Bilbao et al. 2021] Across 16 resistance-training studies, full ROM produced greater strength adaptation than partial ROM and favored functional performance, but evidence for hypertrophy differences was not clearly superior and the dataset was not specific to pulling exercises. [ACSM 2009] Resistance-training outcomes depend on coordinated prescription of exercise selection, intensity, volume, frequency, rest, and progression; this supports programming rows and vertical pulls as adjustable resistance exercises rather than treating EMG differences as outcome guarantees.
output.exercise_family: Rows, pulldowns, pull-ups, and upper-back pulling

results.input: Squats, split squats, lunges, and knee-dominant lower-body work

output.catalog_implications: Evidence-backed fields should encode squat depth, trunk inclination, tibial/knee travel, stance width, foot rotation, load, velocity, unilateral/bilateral status, rear-foot elevation, step length, and whether the feet remain fixed or a landing occurs; these are not cosmetic descriptors because they alter joint moments, ROM, stabilization, and muscle-demand profiles. Evidence supports a planning model in which deeper squats are generally higher-knee-moment and lower-capacity than shallower squats at matched intent, while deep-ROM training has stronger evidence for knee-extensor hypertrophy and some strength/jump adaptations; this is an inference for programming, not a universal prescription. Split squats and lunges should not be collapsed into one mechanical category: stationary split squats avoid the landing phase, whereas walking lunges add deceleration and impact demands. Rear-foot elevation and longer step length can be represented as likely hip-extensor-bias or altered-load-distribution modifiers, but exact bias should remain conditional on torso angle, front-foot position, depth, load, and individual technique. EMG labels should be treated as activation indicators rather than direct evidence of hypertrophy, maximal force, injury prevention, or sport-skill transfer. Limits are substantial: many findings come from small samples of healthy, resistance-trained young adults; comparative studies use different relative loads across exercises; most evidence is acute or short-term; and the 2024 squat paper is a Level-5 clinical commentary. None of these sources directly establishes that squats, lunges, or split squats produce a particular sport skill.
output.direct_findings: [Straub & Powers 2024] Squat demand is modifiable through trunk inclination, tibia position, stance width, foot rotation, and depth; the ground-reaction-force geometry creates flexion moments at the hip and knee that require extensor action, while trunk and torso musculature contribute to stabilization. The review emphasizes that parameter interactions make generic technique claims unreliable. [Cotter et al. 2013] In trained young men, peak external knee-flexion moment increased as both squat depth and load increased; 1RM decreased as depth progressed from above-parallel to parallel and below-parallel, and the usual load reduction at greater depth did not fully offset the increased knee moment. [Bloomquist et al. 2013] In a 12-week, repetition-matched comparison, deep squats to approximately 120 degrees of knee flexion produced greater front-thigh muscle cross-sectional-area gains and larger improvements in selected knee-extension strength and squat-jump performance than shallow squats to approximately 60 degrees; deep training also transferred to shallow 1RM, whereas shallow training transferred less to deep 1RM. [Mackey & Riemann 2021] At the tested relative loads, both Bulgarian split squat and bilateral back squat were hip-dominant, but the Bulgarian split squat showed lower knee moment impulse and peak knee moment than the back squat; the authors identify it as a possible option when emphasizing hip extension while limiting knee demand. [Stastny et al. 2015] Walking lunges and stationary split squats differ mechanically because walking lunges include a dynamic landing/impact phase whereas split squats keep both feet fixed; contralateral-loaded walking lunges produced high eccentric gluteus-medius activity, while carrying position and training status affected EMG and knee/hip ROM. [Neto et al. 2020] The systematic review classified split squats, in-line lunges, traditional lunges, and several squat variants among exercises producing very high gluteus-maximus EMG in the included literature, but it also notes that external load, velocity, fatigue, mechanical complexity, stabilization demands, and EMG normalization influence measured activation.
output.exercise_family: Squats, split squats, lunges, and knee-dominant lower-body work

results.input: Deadlifts, hip hinges, hip thrusts, and posterior-chain work

output.catalog_implications: Evidence-supported catalog fields should distinguish movement pattern (hip-dominant hinge/hip extension), primary joint actions (hip extension with isometric or dynamically controlled trunk and variable knee contribution), and posterior-chain targets (gluteus maximus, hamstrings, spinal extensors, with contribution depending on variant). Treat barbell path, stance, handle position, knee flexion, torso inclination, and range of motion as mechanics-changing modifiers rather than cosmetic cues. Infer that straight-bar deadlifts generally impose more lumbar/hip moment demand than a hex bar at matched relative submaximal loads, while hex-bar variants shift some demand toward the knee; label this as an acute biomechanics inference, not a universal programming rule. Treat hip thrusts as hip-focused with low ankle demand and a nonconstant, phase-dependent external hip moment; do not encode “constant tension” or “maximum tension at lockout” as a high-confidence universal field. RDLs and other straight-legged hinges should be cataloged as lengthened-hip-flexion/hip-extension patterns, but muscle emphasis should remain variant- and technique-dependent rather than assigned from exercise name alone. For fatigue planning, avoid unsupported claims that deadlift repetitions-to-failure predictably alter lumbar mechanics: direct evidence is sparse; use conservative fatigue flags because high loads generate substantial spinal loads and repetitive-lifting studies suggest possible adverse biomechanical changes. For posterior-chain programming, evidence supports progressive, individualized training and a 12–16-week context in chronic-low-back-pain rehabilitation, but that clinical finding should not be generalized to healthy performance populations. No cited source justifies claiming that deadlifts or hip thrusts automatically produce a sport skill; any sprint or horizontal-force-transfer claim should be marked as limited, mixed, and population/protocol dependent.
output.direct_findings: [Deadlift-low-back-review] The reviewed deadlift literature reports heavy-deadlift lumbar compressive loads of approximately 5–18 kN and shear loads of approximately 1.3–3.2 kN; load magnitude, bar design, and participant sex affect lumbar kinetics. The review found no direct studies of low-back biomechanics during repetitive deadlift-to-failure protocols, so repetitive-lifting evidence should not be treated as direct deadlift injury evidence. [Swinton-hex-bar] In trained male powerlifters lifting 10–80% 1RM, the hexagonal bar permitted a higher 1RM and produced lower peak lumbar, hip, and ankle moments but higher knee moments than a straight bar; peak force, velocity, and power were also higher with the hex bar. These are acute, submaximal laboratory findings, not proof of superior long-term adaptation. [Deadlift-EMG-review] The systematic review shows that deadlift variation, stance, load, range, and technique alter EMG outcomes; EMG indicates neural activity, not force, hypertrophy, or injury risk by itself. [Hip-thrust-systematic-review] Across the included studies, hip thrusts generally elicited high hip-extensor activation, often greater gluteus-maximus and biceps-femoris activation than squats, while straight-bar deadlifts produced greater biceps-femoris activation than hip thrusts in a cited comparison. The review found mixed chronic sprint-transfer results, with some positive and some null studies. [Brazil-hip-thrust] At 70% 1RM in 19 trained males, the barbell hip thrust created substantially greater bilateral extensor demand at the hip than at the knee or pelvic-trunk joints, negligible ankle kinetics, and a hip-extensor moment that diminished through the lifting phase rather than remaining constant. [Dicus-hinge-EMG] At 50% estimated 1RM in young healthy males, changing a straight-legged hinge from RDL to cable pull-through reduced activation of longissimus, multifidus, biceps femoris, and semitendinosus, whereas changing RDL to reverse hyperextension increased gluteus maximus, biceps femoris, and semitendinosus activation. [Posterior-chain-meta-analysis] In adults with chronic low-back pain, posterior-chain resistance programs of at least six weeks—particularly 12–16 weeks—improved pain, disability, and strength more than general exercise in the pooled analysis, without a significant difference in reported adverse events; the authors emphasized that the specific optimal deadlift or hip-lift pattern remains uncertain.
output.exercise_family: Deadlifts, hip hinges, hip thrusts, and posterior-chain work

results.input: Cable exercises, flyes, pullover patterns, and resistance-curve variations

output.catalog_implications: Evidence-supported fields should distinguish resistance direction (gravity, single-cable line, dual-cable lines), pulley/anchor height, stance or bench support, grip/handle, shoulder and elbow action, and whether the exercise is a fly/crossover, pullover, pulldown, or row. Evidence supports recording expected joint-moment and muscle-emphasis changes across the range of motion, not labeling a cable exercise as having uniformly constant tension: cable force may be relatively stable while joint torque changes with the moment arm. For flyes, catalog descriptions may classify them as a single-joint horizontal-adduction pattern with lower loadability and potentially higher control/stabilization demands than pressing; this is an inference from acute EMG and mechanics, not proof of superior or inferior hypertrophy. For pullovers, describe shoulder extension/flexion through a range and allow pectoralis-major and latissimus-dorsi emphasis to vary with shoulder angle, cable line, torso orientation, and implement; do not assign a fixed prime-mover ranking across all variants. For variable-resistance variants, record the resistance medium and approximate contribution across ROM, but do not promise greater hypertrophy or universal strength transfer: the meta-analysis concerns maximum strength, mixes bands/chains and exercises, and reports load- and population-dependent effects. Programming models can treat cable and fly/pullover variants as useful for altering line of pull, joint torque distribution, stability demands, and exercise practicality, while preserving the distinction between acute EMG/joint-mechanics evidence and long-term adaptation. Limits are substantial: most direct studies are small, acute, male, resistance-trained samples; EMG is not a direct measure of hypertrophy or force contribution; isometric pullover/pulldown findings do not fully generalize to dynamic repetitions; and the cited studies do not establish that these exercises produce sport skills.
output.direct_findings: [1] Cable resistance acts along the cable direction rather than vertically; in a study comparing bench press, cable crossover/fly, and cable pullover, crossover and pullover showed distinct shoulder joint angles and loading patterns, and increasing the load from 15% to 30% body mass substantially increased maximum joint moments. [1] The crossover exhibited larger fluctuations in shoulder abduction-adduction angle and absolute joint moment than the pullover and bench-press variants. [2] Across lat pulldown, inclined pulldown, seated cable row, and upright row, exercise choice altered shoulder moments and spinal curvature; seated rows produced the highest sagittal-plane moments, while load increases generally shifted joint-moment curves upward. [3] External torque depends on the resistance line of action and the changing moment arm, so cable height, body position, handle path, and joint angle are mechanics fields rather than cosmetic setup details. [4] At 6RM in resistance-trained men, barbell bench press produced greater pectoralis-major, anterior-deltoid, and triceps EMG than dumbbell flyes across most phases, while flyes produced greater biceps EMG; the fly used lower external loads. [5] In a small acute study at 30% body mass, the barbell pullover emphasized pectoralis-major activation more than latissimus-dorsi activation, with the relative emphasis attributed to the external-force lever arm. [6] In maximal isometric comparisons, pullover and pulldown force and myoelectric activity varied materially with shoulder-joint position; pectoralis-major, latissimus-dorsi, and posterior-deltoid EMG were angle-dependent, while perceived exertion did not differ significantly by position or exercise. [7] Across 14 studies, variable-resistance training showed a pooled maximum-strength advantage over constant resistance, but the effect depended on training status and load; among trained subjects, the advantage was observed primarily at loads of at least 80% 1RM, whereas results were null below 80%.

results.input: Rotational, anti-rotation, trunk flexion, and trunk extension exercises

output.catalog_implications: Evidence-supported fields: classify each entry by primary task (active rotation, resisting rotation, flexion, extension), contraction mode (dynamic or isometric), whether lumbar motion is intended, whether hip motion contributes, and whether loading is external, bodyweight, or perturbation-based. Evidence-supported calibration: anti-rotation/bracing entries should be tagged as trunk co-contraction and rotational-displacement-resistance tasks, not as zero-load tasks, because greater stability can carry a compressive penalty [VeraGarcia2007] [Kavcic2004]. Evidence-supported calibration: flexion and extension entries should record ROM intent and hip contribution separately; sit-up and back-extension labels cannot be assumed to isolate the spine because hip motion materially changes activation [Konrad2006]. Evidence-supported planning inference: use low-to-moderate-load isometrics or anti-movement drills when the goal is endurance, control, or reduced spinal excursion, and progressive dynamic flexion/extension when loaded ROM is an explicit objective, while scaling volume for fatigue and technique loss [McGill1998] [Sutanto2022]. Limits: most direct mechanics studies use small samples of healthy adults, surface EMG is not a direct measure of force or hypertrophy, modeled compression/stability depends on assumptions, and the evidence does not establish that any listed exercise transfers to a specific sport skill. The cited evidence is also stronger for bracing and general stabilization than for named anti-rotation exercises such as the Pallof press, so catalog claims for those exercises should remain task-mechanical rather than sport-performance claims.
output.direct_findings: [McGill1998] Exercise selection should balance the need to stress tissues against excessive loading; strength, flexibility, endurance, and spinal stability are distinct programming targets, and some exercises can challenge musculature while minimizing spinal load. [Kavcic2004] Stabilization exercises differ materially in measured muscle activation, lumbar compression, and modeled stability; those variables should be assessed together rather than treating “core” or “stability” as a single exposure. [VeraGarcia2007] Abdominal bracing increased torso co-contraction, reduced lumbar displacement, and increased modeled trunk stability during sudden posterior perturbation, but also increased spinal compression; hollowing was less effective for controlling the perturbation in this protocol. [Konrad2006] Pure spine-flexion exercises such as curl-ups produced greater than 50% MVC abdominal activation, sit-ups increased peak activation when hip flexion was added, while many bridging and back/hip-extension tasks produced less than 35% MVC trunk-extensor activity; combined hip and trunk extension reached about 50% MVC mainly at the end of extension. [Yoo2013] Bracing preferentially activated the internal oblique at about 60% EMGmax, whereas rectus abdominis, external oblique, and erector spinae activity was lower than in selected dynamic flexion or extension exercises. [Sutanto2022] Isometric, motor-control, and isotonic trunk training are meaningfully different categories: isometric work maintains a neutral spine under load, isotonic work moves the lumbar spine through loaded flexion/extension, and motor-control work emphasizes selective deep-muscle activation; in chronic low-back-pain populations, isometric and motor-control interventions improved pain/disability versus controls, but comparative exercise superiority was not consistent.
output.exercise_family: Rotational, anti-rotation, trunk flexion, and trunk extension exercises

results.input: Plyometrics, jumps, throws, sleds, and speed-strength drills

output.catalog_implications: Evidence-supported fields should distinguish the exercise subtype and force-vector emphasis: vertical/horizontal jumps, repeated reactive jumps, ballistic throws, and resisted horizontal sled sprints are not interchangeable. For jumps, catalog mechanics should record eccentric braking or countermovement, amortization/contact-time demand, concentric propulsion, landing exposure, and whether the drill is bilateral, unilateral, vertical, horizontal, or multidirectional. This is an evidence-to-catalog inference grounded in the SSC and RSI literature, not a claim that every drill has the same joint loading. Range-of-motion fields should remain exercise- and intent-specific: deeper countermovements generally change the braking/propulsion strategy, but the cited reviews do not justify one universal depth or landing posture. Programming models should expose contacts/repetitions, distance, load, rest, and quality/fatigue stop rules; high-volume plyometrics can reduce force and rate of force development, while sled prescriptions should specify load as absolute mass and/or percentage of body mass and separate acceleration from maximal-velocity intent. Sled evidence supports acceleration-oriented use more confidently than maximal-velocity transfer, and pooled findings do not establish a universally optimal resistance. Throws should be cataloged as ballistic whole-body or upper-body/trunk power drills with implement mass, direction, release, and catch/no-catch status; the cited power review supports modality classification, not a claim of sport-skill transfer. Overall limits are important: studies are heterogeneous in exercise choice, participant training status, volume, load, and outcome measurement; most plyometric meta-analytic evidence lacks robust control comparisons; sled results are strongest for sprint-test outcomes rather than sport performance; and no cited source supports claiming that a listed exercise directly produces a specific sport skill.
output.direct_findings: [Davies 2015] Plyometric actions comprise eccentric pre-stretch, a brief amortization/time-to-rebound phase, and concentric shortening; shorter transition time allows more effective use of stored elastic energy, while longer delays dissipate energy as heat. The magnitude, rate, and duration of the pre-stretch alter stored energy. [Kons 2023] Across 29 meta-analyses, plyometric training showed trivial-to-large effects on physical-performance outcomes, but the evidence base was weakened because most meta-analyses emphasized pre-to-post changes and only five included control-group comparisons. [Alcaraz 2018] Resisted sled training improved acceleration and full-sprint performance in the pooled pre/post evidence, whereas maximal-velocity improvements were not statistically significant; recommended pooled programming context was approximately 2–3 sessions per week for at least 6 weeks, with more than 160 m per session and about 2680 m total, although load intensity was not a consistent determinant. [Drinkwater 2009] A high-volume acute plyometric bout produced peripheral neuromuscular fatigue with substantial reductions in force and rate of force development, so volume can impair explosive output and requires recovery planning. [Ramirez-Campillo 2023] Plyometric jump training is particularly relevant to reactive-strength-index outcomes, which combine jump performance with ground-contact time; protocols vary substantially, including both fast and slower jump exercises. [Cormie 2011] Ballistic, plyometric, and weightlifting exercises are viable power-training modalities, but power development depends on matching exercise selection, load, movement velocity, and athlete requirements; the review does not establish that a generic drill transfers to a particular sport skill.

results.input: Kettlebell, landmine, battle-rope, and athletic conditioning exercises

output.catalog_implications: Evidence: Kettlebell swings should be cataloged primarily as ballistic hip-hinge exercises with substantial posterior-chain EMG in the studied muscles, while exact activation depends on hand position, technique, hip mobility, load, and participant experience. Inference: classify swings, cleans, and snatches as velocity- and technique-sensitive rather than assigning fixed muscle percentages or assuming universal lumbar/hip effects. Evidence: battle ropes are reliably vigorous metabolic-conditioning tools, and wave pattern changes trunk/shoulder emphasis; gluteal demand is comparatively low in the cited wave protocol. Inference: catalog intensity using work interval, rest interval, rope length/mass, wave style, stance, and cadence—not a nominal exercise label alone. Evidence: landmine loading follows an arc and can reduce vertical force and quadriceps activity relative to a goblet squat while increasing horizontal force; punch throws show load–velocity behavior. Inference: represent landmine exercises as directionally constrained, semi-ballistic or ballistic patterns with exercise-specific ROM and force-vector fields; do not map them as equivalent substitutes for vertical pressing, squatting, or sport actions. Evidence: the consensus statement and battle-rope acute data support meaningful fatigue and recovery costs. Inference: programming models should preserve quality by using conservative early volumes, explicit rest, velocity/technique stop rules for ballistic landmine and kettlebell work, and separate conditioning fatigue from claims of strength or sport-skill adaptation. Limits: most direct mechanics studies use small samples of healthy young adults, acute bouts, surface EMG, or fixed laboratory protocols; evidence is sparse for landmine presses/rows, diverse loads, clinical populations, long-term injury outcomes, and battle-rope range-of-motion comparisons. No cited source establishes that these exercises produce a specific sport skill.
output.direct_findings: [K1] The kettlebell scoping review identified 99 publications but found longitudinal studies generally underpowered and low quality; reported effects were usually trivial to small, with low to very low confidence and weak support for therapeutic prescription. [K2] In healthy young adults, two- and one-handed kettlebell swings produced mean activation of approximately 75% MVIC for gluteus maximus, 55% for gluteus medius, and 79% for biceps femoris; biceps femoris reached peak activation before gluteus maximus and medius. [K2] Passive hip-flexor length correlated moderately with gluteus-maximus activation, so hip position/mobility may alter observed muscle recruitment. [B1] A 10-minute protocol of 15-second double-arm waves and 45-second rests produced mean heart rate of 163 ± 11 bpm, peak oxygen uptake of 35.4 ± 5.4 mL·kg−1·min−1, peak 10.1 ± 1.6 METs, and high acute energy expenditure, consistent with vigorous-intensity conditioning. [B2] During battle-rope waves, anterior deltoid, external oblique, and lumbar erector-spinae activity ranged roughly 51–73% MVIC, whereas gluteus-medius activity was 14–18% MVIC. Unilateral waves increased external-oblique activity, while bilateral waves increased lumbar-erector activity. [B3] In a specific 20-second protocol with a fixed athletic stance, double-arm waves increased vastus medialis oblique, vastus lateralis, rectus-abdominis, and multifidus activity relative to alternating waves, while alternating waves increased gastrocnemius activity; adding whole-body vibration increased EMG, but this does not establish superior long-term outcomes. [L1] Compared with a goblet squat, the landmine squat reduced vastus-medialis/vastus-lateralis activity and vertical forces while increasing posterior horizontal forces, demonstrating that the angled bar path materially changes the force and muscle-demand profile. [L2] Three landmine punch-throw variations were examined for reliability and load–velocity relationships, supporting use as a measurable ballistic resistance exercise; the study does not prove improved punching skill or sport transfer. [C1] The professional consensus on extreme conditioning programs warns that high-intensity, timed/maximal mixed-modal sessions can create excessive overload and fatigue; it recommends progression, monitoring, adequate recovery, and avoiding indiscriminate volume escalation.

results.input: Arms, forearms, calves, scapular control, serratus, and small-muscle accessory exercises

output.catalog_implications: Evidence: Scapular-control and serratus fields should record plane of motion, elevation angle, scapular action (upward rotation, protraction, retraction), humeral rotation, open- versus closed-chain status, and whether the outcome is EMG ratio or external loading [S1] [S2] [S3]. Inference: Catalog entries should label EMG-based activation as a proxy rather than a direct hypertrophy or injury-prevention claim, and should avoid claiming that any drill restores scapular mechanics in symptomatic populations without population-specific evidence. Evidence: Calf entries should distinguish knee-extended versus knee-flexed plantarflexion, gastrocnemius versus soleus emphasis, foot orientation, and ankle ROM or muscle-length region [S4] [S5] [S6]. Inference: A planning model can assign a higher gastrocnemius-long-length and knee-extended emphasis to standing or straight-leg calf raises, while assigning relatively greater soleus practicality to seated/bent-knee work; it should not treat these as exclusive activations. Evidence: Overhead elbow-extension positioning can increase long-head triceps hypertrophy, and ACSM supports small-muscle single-joint work within goal-specific, periodized programming [S7] [S8]. Inference: Arm-accessory fields should capture joint position, especially shoulder position for triceps and forearm orientation/grip for elbow-flexor or wrist/forearm variants, while scheduling them after high-demand compound work when fatigue preservation matters. Limits: The scapular studies are predominantly acute EMG studies in healthy participants; calf interventions are small and population- or sex-specific; the triceps study does not generalize automatically to every exercise, trainee, or clinical population; direct evidence for many isolated forearm, wrist, finger, rotator-cuff, and other small-muscle accessories remains sparse. No cited source supports a claim that these exercises produce a sport skill.
output.direct_findings: [S1] Across healthy-shoulder EMG studies, diagonal and scapular-protraction exercises produced favorable serratus-anterior activation ratios, while prone flexion, high scapular retraction, and prone external rotation with the shoulder abducted and elbow flexed favored lower-trapezius ratios; standing work tended to raise upper-trapezius contribution, particularly through approximately 60–120° of elevation. The review also notes that these are activation-ratio findings, not proof of superior long-term strength or hypertrophy. [S2] Serratus-anterior activation was highest in exercises requiring substantial scapular upward rotation, including shoulder-abduction/elevation tasks. [S3] Scapulohumeral exercises can produce different serratus-anterior EMG levels and external resistance demands; EMG amplitude should therefore be interpreted alongside the actual load and movement configuration. [S4] In young women training calf raises for eight weeks, partial ROM in the initial portion of the excursion, at longer gastrocnemius muscle lengths, produced greater medial-gastrocnemius hypertrophy than full ROM and final-ROM conditions, and greater lateral-gastrocnemius hypertrophy than final ROM. [S5] Twelve weeks of standing, knee-extended calf-raise training produced greater lateral- and medial-gastrocnemius and whole-triceps-surae volume gains than seated, knee-flexed training, whereas soleus gains were similar between conditions. [S6] Nine weeks of altering foot position during calf training produced different regional gastrocnemius hypertrophy responses, supporting the possibility of modest head-specific bias from foot orientation; this does not establish complete isolation of one muscle head. [S7] In trained or recreationally trained adults, elbow-extension training with the arm overhead produced substantially greater triceps-brachii hypertrophy than training with the arm in a neutral position, consistent with a long-muscle-length advantage for the biarticular long head. [S8] For resistance-training programming, the position stand supports bilateral and unilateral single- and multijoint exercises, sequencing larger or multijoint work before smaller single-joint work when preserving intensity is important, multiple-set training for hypertrophy, and load/volume/frequency selection according to goal and training status. It does not prescribe a unique best curl, extension, forearm drill, calf variation, or scapular-control exercise.
